title: Why the first self was afraid
hookLine: the self's first feeling was fear, and seeing ended it
carry: fear comes from seeing a second
tomorrow: say it to the mirror over and over. does that make it true?
last: EVERY NAME COMES AFTER THE I.

cards: Alone in a quiet house at night, every creak sounds like someone. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad puts that feeling at the very start of everything. Right after the self says I am, the text says: it was afraid.
That's the odd detail. Nothing else exists yet. No enemy, no dark forest, no stranger at the door.
So what is there to be afraid of?

teach.b: The text doesn't scold the fear or call it silly. It says that's why a person alone is afraid, tracing that night-time feeling all the way back to the beginning. Then the self thinks it through.
There is nothing here but me.
So what am I afraid of? And at that, the fear left. The text asks once more, in its own voice: of what should it have been afraid?
And it answers with a short line worth keeping: fear comes from a second. So the puzzle solves itself. The self wasn't afraid of anything.
It was afraid the way a person alone in a dark house is afraid, sensing a second where there is none. Fear needs an other: someone who could leave, a thing that could hurt, a face that could judge.

In this story, what ends the fear isn't company, and it isn't courage. It's looking, and seeing that there's no second there at all. Advaita, the school whose name means not-two, hears aham brahmasmi in that light.
If Brahman is what I am, and Brahman is also all this, then at the deepest level nothing out there is wholly a stranger. And the text stays honest.
In its very next lines the self is still not happy. One alone has no delight, it says.
So seeing ends the fear here, but the story isn't finished.

how: Some teachers of Advaita Vedanta read the Brihadaranyaka's line 'fear comes from a second' alongside aham brahmasmi, as a picture of how seeing no separate other ends fear.

o: I am alone: the self's cry in the dark
I am Brahman: the self is the one reality
I fear Brahman: a line of awe before God

games.q: the self's first feeling. tap the pairs.

s: the Upanishads teach that a spiritual person never feels fear
here even the self is afraid at first; the text explains the fear instead of scolding it.
in the story, the self's fear leaves when it sees no second
there is nothing here but me, so what am I afraid of? and the fear left.
once the fear leaves, the story is finished
in the next lines the self still has no delight: one alone has none.

games.q: your little brother is scared of the dark hallway. by the Brihadaranyaka's story, what helps first?
o: turn on the light and look together: no second is there.
tell him fear is silly and he should just stop it.
agree something's out there, and keep the door shut.
games.why: the self's fear left when it looked and saw nothing but itself. the text doesn't scold the fear; it looks.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one thing coming up that makes you nervous. Notice the second in it: the face, the room, the outcome. Then ask the text's question quietly, the way the self did: what am I afraid of?
Don't answer it. Let the question sit while the breath comes and goes.

wordCard.voice: Aham brahmasmi, and the second piece of its story: fear comes from a second, and leaves when no second is seen.

orig.note: Sanskrit dvitiya, a second, an other: the word in 'fear comes from a second'.

carryVoice: The line for the day: fear comes from seeing a second. Day 1745, in the books.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.2 (the self was afraid; so one who is alone is afraid; it thought, since there is nothing but me, of what am I afraid? and its fear left; of what should it have been afraid? fear comes from a second)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.3 (it had no delight; one alone has no delight)
